Author: @HenryLoenwind
Content:
Congestion changes are a bandaid on an untreated wound. The issue of those cities isn't car traffic, it is that there is a need to move an ungodly amount of people each day. To fix traffic means reducing the need for people to travel in the first place, and here the prime culprit is the imbalance between work places and living spaces. If you have three times the number of work places in your city core than you have people living there, you will have traffic.

If the number is balanced, it won't eliminate all traffic, but it will only be a small fraction. You will also still have intra-city traffic as few people work and live and shop in the same building, but the closer those places are to each other, the more other modes of transport become viable. If someone's commute is only three bus stops away from their home, they will take the bus....or even walk. But the longer the commute becomes, the more a door-to-door solution appeals to people. It often is faster, taking into account having to switch between different bus/tram/subway/train lines, and the comfort of sitting in your own well upholstered seat, listening to your own stereo system, cannot be ignored as travel times become longer than about 15 minutes.

Content:
Ever since the talk of congestion pricing entered public discourse this year, I’ve been dying to talk about the solution used by the city in second place in the driving delay chart shown by Wendover, Mexico City.

With it certain cars can’t be on the road on certain days of the week depending on your license plate, for example a license plate that ends in 5 or 6 can’t drive on Mondays. Newer cars that meet emissions standards and hybrid or electric cars are exempt from these rules.

These rules apply (kinda) to all vehicles in Mexico. I don’t live in Mexico City but I still have to do emissions testing every 6 months and my plate is assigned a pretty color depending on its final digit. 

These rules along with the aggressive driving in Mexico City have, at least to me, made me never think of driving over there. Mexico City’s transportation system is good enough (at least for a non-resident), you can get by just by using the Metro and Metrobús (an for like a tenth of the price!).

Author: @Emelec35
Content:
As someone who’s lived their whole life in the city and learned how to drive in midtown Manhattan, there’s a couple massive flaws with congestion pricing — the alternatives. 

The Subways are CONSTANTLY delayed, all hours of the day. I think part of the reason is how old the system is, and the constant need to update and renovate tracks, cars, stations, etc. The entire system is decrepit. The other issue that leads to train delays is safety. This one I think is the most obvious (just look at mainstream media). But the subway is incredibly unsafe. The subway is averaging 1-3 deaths PER DAY… which is unsustainable in any city. Now many of the safety factors are do to terrible NYC legislation rather than the MTA, but there needs to be coordination between the city, the MTA, and NYPD to make the subways safer, especially since rider numbers should (in theory) go up with congestion pricing. 

The other issue that goes under the radar is the bus system. The bus system works very effectively in lower density areas that are outside of the subways range (think further out in queens, BK, etc.), however in higher density areas like Manhattan, they are an absolute disaster. Firstly the bus lanes go unused. Take 2nd ave for example. The bus lanes frequently have cars either parked or double parked in them which means the buses have to go back into the normal traffic lanes. This means that the city effectively REMOVED an entire lane out of the equation, therefore bottlenecking all the traffic into 2 lanes  . Now you can pin it on the double parked cars, but people forget to install the bus lanes the city removed parking space, and not just any parking space, COMMERCIAL parking space. So every morning m-f these trucks and vans still need to make their deliveries. You can’t blame one party for this but I honestly can’t see the need for bus lanes if they’re not being enforced or even used. 

Then comes gridlock, and the bus driver superiority complex. Any NYC driver will understand what I’m talking about, but bus drivers DON’T PLAY. You see bus drivers are practically invincible when it comes to the rules of the road, they can’t get speeding tickets, red light tickets, or gridlock tickets. They also cannot be found liable in accidents (in very rare circumstances they can, but they are heavily protected by the city). 

What I’m getting at is bus drivers drive worse than most city car drivers. Often during rush hour they are responsible for gridlock, they’ll drive through red lights and stick out blocking the opposing/cross traffic. They’ll back up traffic for 6-10 blocks simply because the rules don’t apply to them. Now I don’t know how you’d solve them, because they do service a community in Manhattan that can’t access the subways (disabled, elderly, etc.) but I think the solve comes from making the subways more accessible in higher density parts of the city, and decreasing the bus routes during rush hour in higher density areas. The reality is in Manhattan, the streets are too small for a normal sized bus, and WAY TOO small for the extended “double buses”

There’s a reason the MTA’s approval and safety ratings are at an all time low.  Everything on paper sounds good, but when you’re in it, it’s a completely different equation. I don’t think congestion pricing is going to be a good idea unfortunately, especially since the alternatives are a logistical nightmare

Author: @stu729
Content:
New Yorker, Staten Islander to be specific. Often transit to this outer borough is difficult and time consuming at best and infuriating at least. For years there was no way to get back home without paying a toll, be it by bridge, mass transit, or ferry. The ferry was made free only in the late 90s. And the tolls on the crossings only go up and up.

While working in the city, Express bus routes home would often stop running as early as 6pm. Working late meant finding an alternative route through a combination of other Express bus routes, local buses, and just walking because the half hour wait between one local bus and another would take just as long as walking. Even if the express buses were running, you run the risk of overcrowded buses or buses running well behind schedule. There were times where a trip home from midtown starting around 10pm could take in excess of 2 hours compared to a 40 minute car ride at that hour. My personal record was about 3 hours, an hour waiting for the closer bus before giving up and taking a different one, an hour on that bus, and then an hour walk because the connecting local bus never showed. 

If the MTA could be trusted to expand express bus service to the outer boroughs, including this Forgotten Borough, them maybe this scheme could work. The sad and admittedly cynical expectation is that the MTA will focus on some improvements within the city proper, but leave Staten Island out in the cold again, and we will still be driving in because the alternative is not always that much better.

Author: @derpydestinies
Content:
Usage per mile, when you have dedicated bus lanes, and buses running every 15-30mn, the lanes dedicated for said traffic are barely used and thus cost for this is much higher per vehicle transported thus less efficient.

 One thing very few people discuss in pro congestion pricing: implementation pre-covid  to present day of traffic slowing and volume restricting traffic patterns (removing lanes; purposefully inefficient light patterns; allowing more and more rideshare vehicles in the road over the last 10 years which are cars that are always in traffic as they do not have a destination where they park, unlike a commuter; etc) which inherently (and purposefully) cause traffic. I.e., we implemented rules to cause traffic and use the results to argue for tolls to reduce traffic. It's nonsensical. 

There should be things done to reduce pollution (a better infrastructure to support EVs; limiting road closures for festivals like San Gennaro which causes major impacts to traffic and quality of life for those in the neighborhood; ways to bypass the surface roads for people aiming to go from Jersey to Brooklyn/Queens and vice versa(aka, tunnels)). This, though, is putting the cart before the horse as the MTA is and has always been poorly managed and their service is not up to par with the rest of the world. 
The money collected for congestion pricing will take decades to actually make a meaningful (if any) impact, as time and time again, MTA projects end up costing multiples of the original estimates. Fix the MTA. Then fund the new fancy projects. We really need to get back to the basics. 

Ultimately, you will see (negative) unintentional consequences with this and many will regret it. But hey, at least the people on billionaire row will be able to move about the city easier.  😂

Author: @r3laps3
Content:
Wow, Wendover - your videos are usually really insightful but you missed the joke big time on this one.

The "congestion" has been created/hugely exacerbated by the following things:
- removing car lanes in favor of bike lanes
- creating bus-only lanes (sometimes more than one on an avenue!)
- huge number of ride-share cars, which have risen above the TLC cap due to exemptions for electric and handicapped vehicles
- lack of enforcement for constant double parking by both cars and delivery trucks (who bulk settle tickets at highly discounted rates)
- outdoor dining sheds, which contribute to double-parking problems
- vision zero initiatives, which added seconds of delay to *each step* of traffic light cycles at most lights...
- ...and lowered the speed limit, enforced 24/7 since 2022 with school zone speed cameras even well outside school hours (big revenue generator)
- lack of enforcement against drivers entering and blocking intersections they can't clear (aka gridlock)
- closure of roads for UN sessions, high profile visitors, special events, parades, street fairs, summer streets, etc. (meaning it happens a lot)

(Some of these are illustrated in the clips shown in your video!)

We can debate the merit of each - but they all have made things worse even with the same number of cars on the street, except the higher number of TLC vehicles which only adds stress to the whole system.  Those vehicles *already* pay a congestion charge, or rather make their customers pay a congestion charge per ride.  That clearly didn't have any impact, so I am skeptical that adding a redundant fee will further impact anything except price inflation.  Also, there will be major populations that don't pay - that are of course related to government and special interests with a strong lobby.

You did not speak to the impact of the changes in traffic patterns which will likely cause choke points outside the congestion zone.  The expected result will be expansion of the zone to address those new problem areas once that occurs.  If the number of vehicles traveling to the CBD actually does drop, the congestion revenue will also drop and that will be the reason cited to raise the charge in the future.

I'm a daily user of mass transit, obviously against congestion pricing, but kind of want to see it go into effect just so that everyone can see how much of a sham it actually is.  The people talking about how the MTA mismanages their budget are entirely correct.  Giving them more money will not solve that root problem.  Unfortunately it turns out that adding another regressive tax on law abiding citizens is easier than enforcing the law for those who evade subway and bus fares, use fake temp plates/license plate obstruction devices to avoid tolls, illegally block limited travel lanes, etc.  Addressing those existing problems would provide the substantial revenue needed.

Author: @Muninnnr
Content:
It's the same story everywhere: the people complaining about congestion pricing are the (often somewhat wealthy) people who live in suburbs and communities outside of the city itself who use their cars to get in because it's convenient, while the people who actually live in the city and who experience the most direct downsides of having all these cars around approve of it. And unfortunately, it's often the wealthy suburbanites who tend to be catered to.
After the success story in Stockholm, Sweden's second largest city Gothenburg also implemented congestion pricing and as far as I'm concerned it's been a smashing success. Use of public transport is up and parking lots all over the city have been (or are currently being) removed and replaced with more productive areas like parks, housing or sports fields. The removal of parking and the introduction of congestion pricing has obviously made a lot of wealthy suburbanites pissed, but I say screw them. They decided to live outside of the city, so why should they get to decide how the very cities they hate are dealing with the traffic problem?

Author: @oliverrh
Content:
Hey! Brooklyn resident, & trades worker who uses his car for work in Manhattan.

I’m pro-bike, pro-transit funding, & here for a version of congestion pricing. Here’s the issue with the system as proposed:

I can’t take the subway to my work. More specifically, the two saws, small chansaw, pneumatic pruners & various other very sharp tools I use to keep NYC trees from braining people can’t take the subway. 

Setting aside the absolute terror my 28ft saw would give the average subway commuters; I could not carry this stuff without a vehicle. That’s not mentioning the sanitization chemicals, soil testing equipment & various other things I need to do my job that wouldn’t fit in a backpack.

And, for those of you who think you could hire someone in Manhattan to do this: lol you cannot. My company is short staffed & we regularly have to turn down contracts because we can’t hire anyone in the area, even offering full training.

And frankly, while what I do IS important, I am not at the top of the list of people who keep the entirely-made-of-concrete city from literally collapsing around you. Masons, carpenters, materials engineers- every step you take in Manhattan is the result of hundreds, if not thousands of folks work that you never see.

Infrastructure is already suffering in Manhattan because of the way things are currently structured, and I worry that folks who work white-collar jobs in the city don’t understand how much maintenance it takes to keep their home structurally sound.

Look, I’m happy to deal with limitations (possibly similar to how school subway passes work) where work vehicles are only authorized to come in for free on days they’re working a city contract (something that could be proportioned based on existing records in city contracts that lay out how many people of each role will be on site for any given work day) With cars expected to pay congestion pricing coming into the city on days they’re not working. 


If this doesn’t happen; I’ve already told my boss I can’t afford to work in Manhattan if congestion pricing goes in under the current model. I’m already spending about  1 & 1/2 hours of my 8 hours daily pay on existing tolls, fees, and average of the nonsense tickets Manhattan NYPD use to round out their quotas. If the city gives passes to its office workers, it needs to figure out the same for the folks who actually physically fix this city. Otherwise you’re going to end up with more of the current situation; contractors hiring desperate folks without the needed expertise to do essential jobs, putting both those workers and the people who live in Manhattan at increasing risk of disaster.

Author: @Bill_Oddie_Face_Mask
Content:
As someone who has been commuting to NYC to work for years and is now leaving the region entirely, I can tell you everything about commuting to NYC sucks. Driving in is a nightmare due to traffic and lack of parking, Ubering is cripplingly expensive, and the public transit system is simply horrid. The city itself has been in a long decline. 

Congestion pricing works in theory. Fewer people on the road means less traffic so people who need to drive in and cannot rely on traisn (or simply disdain the MTA) can do so more easily. And the money from congestion tolls can be used to make sweeping improvements to the rail system.

In practice it never works. Just look at London, another city in decline. Their transit system isn’t in a much better state than NY’s and traffic is still atrocious. 

The bigger problems are: 
1) most of the money will be used to increase administrative salaries not increased and enhanced commuter rail services
2) 25mph speed limits are ridiculous. And I only use that r word because the more appropriate r word is not Youtube-friendly. 
3) cycle lanes and outright road closures are ubiquitous, squeezing drivers into tighter spaces.

Cars in the absence of government stupidity are the best form of transport. You can arrive and leave on your own schedule, carry your belongings without difficulty, and travel at your own pace. 

With government stupidity, everything sucks, but cars suck slightly less than the alternatives. 

You want to fix pollution? Reopen hudson yards to freight rail, curtail intercity trucking, get rid of all buses and school buses, and get rid of all the cycle lanes and open up all the roads to get cars moving freely in and out of the city. The longer they sit still idling in traffic, the more smog they create as a unit. When they are moving quickly the exhaust is spread more thinly over a wider area and there is no smog.

Author: @billhayes3219
Content:
I wish they would have started by adding a toll to the Brooklyn Bridge instead.  (It's the only Manhattan bridge that has no fee to drive on)  Brooklyn travelers going into Manhattan or Queens hit enormous delays until they pass the exit for the Brooklyn Bridge. (And to a lesser degree, Brooklyn bound travelers)  Everyone has already sat through this traffic anyway, so many drivers think:"What's a few more minutes to squeeze onto the Brooklyn Bridge if I can save ~$14?".  Of course,  this makes traffic worse for everyone, as everyone tries to pack into the right lane at the last minute.

After the Brooklyn Bridge, traffic (usually) disappears, and they can travel into Queens for free, or into Manhattan via tunnel for a full price toll.

For myself personally, when I travel from Brooklyn into Manhattan, I would be willing to pay the toll for the Tunnel in order to shorten my trip.  But I don't have that choice, because of the persistent bottleneck on the highway.  When I go to Queens, I take residential streets, which is just as bad of an experience.

As you mentioned, the congestion pricing is a disproportionate cost on the middle and lower class.  Adding a Brooklyn Bridge toll would generate revenue, spread out traffic flow, and not affect the poor disproportionately. It would additionally benefit drivers who are traveling only between Queens and Brooklyn.

Also: everyone is skeptical that any increased revenue will actually benefit public transit, but that's a whole other topic.

I think the real problem is that you have 8.6 million people living in an area about 304 square miles.  You can move everybody onto public transport and you're still going to have congestion. 2.  You're also charging more to move goods and services into the city.  This is going to get passed on to consumers.  From my outside perspective, NYC is already expensive enough to live in.  This will only make it more expensive.

3.  From my outside perspective, NYC has a lot of other problems that need fixing, and I don't see either the city or the state spending that money on anything other than their own pet projects.  Any through traffic going north on I-95 is forced across the George Washington Bridge and only the Cross Bronx Expressway.  One way to fix that would be to build and actual bypass and get the through traffic out of NYC.

Author: @tgp528
Content:
As someone who currently lives in NJ and used to live in NYC, this is a good video in practice, and honestly I do agree with most of your points that you've mentioned on how congestion charges would reduce traffic. While I am also for congestion charges, there are some counterpoints that are to note (with solutions that would be unpopular with NY residents):

1. Public transportation in NYC, while better than most of the US, still lacks compared to the rest of the world. The main cause of this issue: Prices Are Too Low. No matter the time of day or the distance traveled, the cost to ride on the MTA remains around $3. Compared to London, Washington DC, and other areas, they lose out by not charging extra to riders based on the "rush hour" traffic. Of course, for NYC people, increasing this fare from $2.25 to $2.50 caused a massive uproar in the community, so I doubt they'd ever be able to implement this. But, (and I could be wrong) the average price in London or DC is around $6-8, and that's with less people traffic than the MTA has on a daily basis. 

2. Public transportation outside NYC is in complete shambles, also due to a lack of funding. Amtrak + NJ Transit has had numerous issues during volatile weather temperatures as the systems are over 80 years old and haven't been modernized in this new climate. The trains don't run fast, and the busses are few and far in between, with numerous delays causing the perception of the transit system to be low among NJ and other NY folks. On top of that, the stations themselves are breaking down, flooding, or not in service due to the lack of funds that can be deployed to fix the infrastructure surrounding NYC. 

The solution is simple, put more money towards the city infrastructure. Residents may suffer in the short-term, but the long-term gains are immense. It's a bigger issue than a simple congestion pricing fix (although we still need that). If this passes, it helps improve the livelihoods for future generations, but it's tough to think that far ahead, which is where politicians should come in and help.

Author: @MichaelNYCBroker
Content:
This is a gross misrepresentation of the topic.  This is a money grab – period.  The transit system loses billions and now even more because of unfettered and unenforced fare jumping. Bridge and tunnel tolls are in excess of $20.00 and parking typically starts at $600/month.  Almost all the toll money already goes to the transit system – not for improvements, but to cover waste, fraud, and mismanagement.  

The street “congestion” since COVID is far less.  The traffic stems from reconfigured pedestrian malls and bike lanes that have choked off the capacity of city streets.  With fewer cars coming in, the city is simply looking for more revenue from fewer people rather than crack down on mass transit mismanagement and waste.  

The claims about office space in Manhattan are technically true, but realistically false insofar as vacancy rates are at record levels due to working from home. Many Class A buildings are at 10% of pre-COVID levels.  Unlike LA, air quality in NYC is excellent, the eco-angle is a false flag.    

The city is trying to get more revenue, and they want it from people they perceive to have no choice in the matter.  As with their onerous tax policies, it will only serve to drive people and businesses away.  And the more they try to take from the few that remain, the more that will leave.

Author: @Borkon
Content:
An acquaintance of mine did some minor work on the software for the tolls in Stockholm. The moment this became known the wider group of friends and colleagues that we were in he ended up feeling so unwelcome that he lost contact with most of us. Some people openly insulted him and he mentioned even receiving death threats. To say that the congestion tax was unpopular is an understatement.

It wasn't helped by IBM failing to implement number plate image recognition on time and the initial rollout incorrectly identified most of the cars. They compensated for their incompetence by introducing an outright evil process for enforcement: drivers were responsible for keeping track of how much they owe and there was no way to find out that information, if you don't pay in time there are no reminders, it goes straight to an enforcement agency. After a while they introduced transponders you could have in your car. Those that ordered the transponders and were unlucky enough to have the post truck pass through the tolls suddenly found themselves with a nasty letter from the debt enforcement agency (because the post truck with your transponder counted as you going through the tolls) and had to go to court to demand a picture of their car as evidence and got a picture of the roof of the post truck. Most didn't go to court and just paid. 

Also, because this was a congestion tax and tax decisions are government decisions and were at that time not exempt from freedom of information requests you could track people by requesting every time and date they passed through the tolls from the tax agency. At least one person was caught cheating when his wife used this method. Sweden had to change the actual constitution to fix that little problem.

Maybe the system is liked now. I guess it's just one of those things that just is and no one cares anymore. Although I suspect that we'd hate the city today if it didn't exist. Now there are serious moves to remove traffic from some of the worst streets in the city and it looks like it's working, people aren't against it and the few pedestrian only streets during the summer are immensely successful.

Author: @LachieWappet
Content:
The efficacy of congestion pricing is actually quite low. Many commenters have said this already, but the only solution to car traffic is viable alternatives to driving – yes, even in Manhattan, which already has arguably the best alternatives to driving of any area in the US. The success of this initiative hinges almost entirely on how the funding is used to improve public transit service.

I highly recommend anyone interested check out "Transport for Suburbia" by Paul Mees for more, but his analysis (albeit over a decade old now) of London's congestion pricing shows that the stronger factor contributing to reduced traffic congestion was increased bus ridership. A component of which can be attributed to the implementation of the congestion charge, sure, but bus ridership in London was already trending upwards in the years preceding the introduction of the charge – and car trips into central London were already declining. 

Paul Mees:
"Those hailing the success of congestion charging also omitted to mention that peak-period car trips to central London had been declining for a long time, with a 13 per cent fall recorded between 1990 and 2000 despite a small rise in travel by all modes. Overall, it seems reasonable to conclude that the London congestion charge and associated bus improvements accelerated this trend, and transferred up to 100,000 car trips per day, plus some rail trips, to bus. The reduction in car trips deserves to be counted as a success, but a modest one. There were 11 million daily car trips across Greater London in 2001, so the result was a reduction of under 1 per cent. Given that Livingstone cited survey evidence pointing to a 4 per cent mode shift from the car to public transport by 2004, perhaps more attention should be given to the measures that produced the other three-quarters of this change. Congestion charging may have a role to play in building sustainable urban transport systems, but it is unlikely to be a major one."

Content:
I have no argument with the benefits of reducing car traffic, but as a long time NYer I'm compelled to give some context to the opposition argument:

1. Almost everyone who *can* avoid driving in the congestion zone already does, because of the hellish nature of driving in Manhattan. Only the people who have to work in the congestion zone, because they can't work remotely, are left, and those are disproportionately working class people who live in areas of both NY and NJ that are underserved by public transit. The MTA's own projections were for traffic to drop only by 10%.

2. Manhattan is not London, a landlocked mid-density sprawl with ring roads around it. It is an extremely dense island in an estuary with only three exits across the Hudson to mainland USA. Two of these are in the congestion zone. The third, the George Washington Bridge, is a lengthy detour if you're coming from / going to the most populated areas to the southwest of the city and will increase traffic and pollution specifically for the lower-income communities in Upper Manhattan and the Bronx. 

3. People in the New York area have been dealing with constant fare increases from the MTA and regional transportation systems in recent years, as well as increased tolls on the bridges and tunnels AND new tolls on the interborough crossings in the last ten years, while public transportation keeps getting less reliable. Where is the money going?

Author: @duncanbuchanan218
Content:
London is instructive in a couple of ways. The area covered was focussed on the congested core and the time of operation were initially set to support the night time economy - it started at 7am and ended ended at 6pm. Second, the area covered was the dense core of the city.
After a few years the zone was increased in size - really to raise money for the city government using congestion as a fig leaf to impose the tax. That extension in to a large more residential area was very unpopular (it was seen for what it was, a tax grab). That mayor lost an election and the increased zone size was removed.
The cost has gone up, now £15 per day, and it applies on weekends now too. The 6pm is still in place and it is largely non-controversial.
BUT, the whole area is as badly congested as ever (probably worse) because even though traffic has fallen 29% since 2003 the road network has been managed to restrict traffic flow - this has particularly impacted bus services and taxi operation.
Focusing on commercial vehicles will be a mistake - they are there to work and any costs imposed just become a tax on the work being done - making your city more expensive.

Author: @user-tb9nr5id5y
Content:
Congestion Pricing isn't about the out of lower Manhattan commuter who values their time highly subsidizing the costs of the out of lower Manhattan commuters who value their time less highly by contributing to the latter's cost of public transportation.  It is about the out of lower Manhattan commuters who value their time high enough to pay congestion pricing subsidizing the public transportation costs of those already in lower Manhattan.  Because little of the money being raised by congestion pricing initiatives will be going to offset the increased transportation costs of those who are outside of lower Manhattan and who will now be needing to shift over to public transportation.

My guess is that few of those driving to Manhattan want to deal with the traffic and parking hassles.  So why do they do it?  1) They don't live within a convenient distance of a mass transit option; 2) The closest mass transit option to them does not go where they want to go, necessitating one or more changes to get there or having to travel further to a mass transit option that gets them where they want to go; 3) The mass transit options available take too long to get them to their destination; 4) Safety concerns, both on the transit and getting to and from the transit.  Dealing with problems 1 and 2 mean providing more parking options at outlying transit points so that people can either park or can use Kiss and Ride.  However most urban planners decry providing these temporary or daily parking nodes because it frustrates other urban planning agendas.

Congestion pricing works in places like London because those who back it simply do not care about how it impacts those outside the zone.  Manhattan's situation is different.  It may be an island, but it is still economically tied to a much larger region.  A region more tied to cars and trucks than those who live in lower Manhattan.  Disincentivizing people from coming to lower Manhattan in private vehicles may mean they won't come at all.

Author: @shawnmou9600
Content:
I live in upper Manhattan, and congestion pricing isn't my preferred solution to transit under-investment. Considering the cost-of-living crisis, I would rather incentivize public transit use rather than directly discourage car use. I do recognize that at some level, both are necessary, but at the same time, transit for people commuting from out of the city is currently not adequate, and I believe that problem needs to be addressed before (or alongside) increasing the cost of driving. As for the problem of raising capital for, I simply think the more sound and equitable solution is to raise taxes on the wealthiest businesses and individuals in the region who benefit the most from the value created by commuters; however, since this seems politically practically impossible, I am in favor of the current plan. I just worry that increasing the cost of travel in one of the most expensive parts of the country without immediately demonstrating the improved alternatives will only garner resentment for city government and the MTA.

In short, I do support congestion pricing, I just wish there was political will to have the wealthiest New Yorkers pitch in to make the improvement of public transit happen in tandem with the discouragement of car-use.

Content:
I'd like to share a nuanced opinion. I'm from Hudson county NJ and nobody supports the congestion tax here. Only NY transplants and vocal transit-activists really want to see this happen.

Author: @dontbanmebrodontbanme5403
Content:
Like anything else, I'll roll with the punches. However, I personally don't like the congestion pricing and my guess is it's something that might get Hochul canned when the next election rolls around.

The problem I have with this is there's a lot of "collateral damage". What about people that are just passing by and are not going into the heart of Manhattan? Say you're coming from Washington Heights and you just want to get to Hoboken. The most logical way to do that is to hop on the Lincoln Tunnel. Or the person coming from Yonkers that needs to hop on the Holland Tunnel? They're just "passing by". And yes, they're supposed to get a reduction of $3 (during peak hours), but I just came up with two scenarios where there is no public transit option, at least not one that's practical. If you're coming from, I don't know, Chappaqua, NY and you want to get to Hoboken NJ, your public transportation option is:

* hop on the metro north and an hour later (and $14.50 later), you're in Grand Central Station
* Either take the #7 train (at another $2.75) or a 15 minute walk over to the port authority
* Take one of their buses for $4, which will take you another 20 minutes or so, not including the time waiting before the bus actually waits for passengers, before leaving the port authority

So $21.25 and probably 2 1/2 hours of your time later, you're in Hoboken, NJ. Of course, if you were carrying bags and other items with you, this makes that journey all the more painful.

I guess the bright side is that drive will have less traffic, so an extra $6 to speed through the few minutes you're in Manhattan might be worth it.

Author: @vaillencourt
Content:
The real solution to the traffic congestion problem in NYC and every other major city is work-from-home. Virtually none of those hundreds of thousands of office workers who commute into the city each day from the suburbs are doing anything in those office buildings that they couldn't do just as well at home instead. To that end, I actively oppose anything that lets people pay to drive on less congested roads. I *want* the billionaire hedge fund manager in his Rolls Royce to have to lose some of his precious time sitting in traffic behind a janitor in a 1990s Honda. I want the people in charge of making decisions about the future of offices to be exposed to the maximum amount of inconvenience possible if they choose to perpetuate the office paradigm.

Instead of congestion pricing, I'd rather the city introduce an office worker tax, where companies were charged a certain amount for each employee who is required to report to an office for a job that could be performed remotely. Ultimately, the concept of the urban office building is obsolete in the age of near-universal access to high speed internet, and the use of urban offices needs to be recognized as a socially deleterious practice that exists now only as a status symbol for companies, rather than a driver of economic growth.

The problem I have with the theory side of congestion pricing is that it's one of those things in economics where it considers people's lives as being in a featureless void where decisions can be made perfectly rather than in truth where it's all sticky and messy. Author: @theotheronethere4391
Content:
A big part of this is geography. As currently constructed, east-west traffic from LI to NJ (and vice versa) almost always result in someone driving right into lower/midtown Manhattan. Either the Lincoln Tunnel to the Midtown Tunnel or the Holland Tunnel to the East River bridges.

Most cities partially solve that by building ring roads to divert traffic away from the city core. The problem is that NYC due to its island geography functionally has no ring road to divert traffic away from the city core. There have been plans in the past to do so, but they always require extremely expensive infrastructure to complete (like the Long Island Sound link).

In turn, there are two routes that serves as "ring roads" around Manhattan but they are each very flawed. One is north via the Cross Bronx Expressway (GWB to NJ, Throngs Neck Bridge to LI) which already is one of the most congested routes in the USA and is both capacity constrained and obsolete from a freeway design philosophy. It can ill afford to pick up any diverted traffic. The 2nd route is south via the BQE to the VZ Bridge to the SIE. However, that will require going through the infamous BQE promenade section, a dangerously obsolete section (everyone agrees it will collapse soon, but NYC did nothing about it for 2+ and counting decades). NYC has actually closed 1 lane in each direction in order to kick the can down the road resulting in 24/7 congestion each way. That path also can ill afford to pick up any diverted traffic.

With both routes north and south functionally blocked, the result is to drive into Manhattan. Take a person from Queens wanting to catch a flight in Newark, the answer is to cross Manhattan. Vice versa, someone from Newark wanting to catch a flight at LGA, the answer, drive into Manhattan. Not sure congestion charge will do anything that...

Author: @connorparadis4804
Content:
I'm a Brooklyn resident and I'm looking forward to its implementation. If it doesn't work as intended, we can always repeal it. But something needs to be done and I like the idea of putting a very direct cost of driving into the zone with the proceeds benefitting transit. You'll almost certainly see more drivers staying on the West Side Highway and FDR to avoid the tolls who otherwise would opt to drive on one of the North/South avenues, which (hopefully) makes getting to destinations within the zone easier/faster/better. Fingers crossed!

At a $9 charge, I don't know if you'll really see commuters opt for commuter rail over driving. NJ Transit and Metro North tickets are already $15+ at peak times (per person). We really need NJ and NY state governments to make the train the more attractive option. Just my two cents, but if commuter rails transitioned to a fareless (or maybe $1 fare) funding system, it would do more to get people on transit than congestion pricing will. Politically, it will never happen, but we can dream.

Author: @PalmelaHanderson
Content:
The ONLY way to solve traffic is to remove as many cars from the road as possible that don't need to be there. Adding more lanes doesn't help, removing bike lanes doesn't help, making lanes wider doesn't help. The only way to achieve that goal is to provide people other options than driving to get where they need to go - protected bike lanes, reliable public transit that doesn't share the road with cars (why take the bus if the bus also gets stuck in traffic with everybody else), etc. If all of that doesn't work... use the stick. Enact policies that artificially make driving more of a pain in the ass. Eliminate on-street parking like they do in Tokyo and they're doing now in Paris. Create "superblocks" like they did in Barcelona, where every street forces you onto collector roads (only bikes and pedestrians can walk through a neighborhood, everyone who doesn't live there has to go around it).

Making everything slightly more inconvenient for drivers will ultimately make things better for everybody, but it has to be coupled with making alternative options to driving better.

Author: @LynxChan
Content:
The idea that a congestion charge is "fair"  is absurd on its face. By definition it's a flat tax rather than a progressive tax - ie it's going to be more painful for the poor than the rich.
Arguing it from individual value of time is just changing the currency from money to time. Poor people are less likely to be able to afford property and are more likely to be poorly served by public transportation, so the pressure to pay the charge, even if painful, is greater for the poor than the rich.

If you think the charge is worth doing anyway that's fine, but own that you are willing to disproportionately impact people with less money, because that is 100% what you are doing

Content: There is another way that congestion on roads occurs.  The reason traffic is so bad in downtown Atlanta is the Grady Curve. What happens is that some drivers who might not be as familiar with this section of highway tap their brakes, or suddenly realize that they have to get over to exit onto 20.  This tapping of the brakes cascades back into traffic compounding as it does.  It gets to the point that traffic further back comes to a complete stop, and this happens literally every day, even outside of rush hour.
